added_lemmas.statement: For every pair \( (A,B) \) of normalized \(2\times2\) probability tables on \(D^2\) for which \(F(A,B)\neq\varnothing\), and every \((c,d)\in F(A,B)\), the handle \(Hthr\) constructs a finite model \(M\in MC(A,B)\) with \(D\)-valued roots \(U0,V0\), a private root \(W0\) having at most eight support points, mutually independent roots, and one deterministic outcome function \(fY\) shared by all regimes, such that \(q=a+b-c+d\). The construction reproduces all four cells of \(A\) and all four cells of \(B\), including on every support face where one or more natural-treatment strata or experimental rows have probability zero.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix normalized probability tables \(A,B\) and a pair \((c,d)\in F(A,B)\). Since the entries of each table are nonnegative and sum to one, the definitions of \(p,r,a,b\) give
\[
0\le p\le1,\qquad 0\le r\le1,
\qquad 0\le a\le p,
\qquad 0\le b\le r,
\]
and also
\[
0\le A(1,1)\le1-p,
\qquad
0\le B(1,1)\le1-r.
\]
The four numbers
\[
w00=pr,\quad w01=p(1-r),\quad
w10=(1-p)r,\quad w11=(1-p)(1-r)
\]
are therefore nonnegative and sum to one.

Define the four prospective success numerators
\[
n_{00}:=c,\qquad n_{01}:=a-c,\qquad
n_{10}:=b-c,\qquad n_{11}:=d.
\]
Membership in \(F(A,B)\) means
\[
\max\{0,a-w01,b-w10\}\le c
\le\min\{w00,a,b\},qquad 0\le d\le w11.
\]
Consequently,
\[
0\le n_{00}=c\le w00,
\]
\[
0\le n_{01}=a-c\le w01,
\qquad
0\le n_{10}=b-c\le w10,
\]
and
\[
0\le n_{11}=d\le w11.
\]
In particular, if \(w_{ij}=0\), the two inequalities \(0\le n_{ij}\le w_{ij}\) force \(n_{ij}=0\). Hence the following definition never divides by zero:
\[
t_{ij}:=
\begin{cases}
n_{ij}/w_{ij},&w_{ij}>0,\\
0,&w_{ij}=0.
\end{cases}
\]
For every \((i,j)\in D^2\), one has \(0\le t_{ij}\le1\) and, in both branches,
\[
w_{ij}t_{ij}=n_{ij}.
\]
Likewise set
\[
\gamma_A:=
\begin{cases}
A(1,1)/(1-p),&1-p>0,\\
0,&1-p=0,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\gamma_B:=
\begin{cases}
B(1,1)/(1-r),&1-r>0,\\
0,&1-r=0.
\end{cases}
\]
The displayed table inequalities imply \(0\le\gamma_A,\gamma_B\le1\). They also imply, including in the null-row branches,
\[
(1-p)\gamma_A=A(1,1),
\qquad
(1-r)\gamma_B=B(1,1),
\]
because \(1-p=0\) forces \(A(1,1)=0\), and \(1-r=0\) forces \(B(1,1)=0\).

On a product probability space with law \(\mathbb P\), let \(U0,V0\) be independent \(D\)-valued roots with
\[
\mathbb P(U0=0)=p,\qquad \mathbb P(V0=0)=r,
\]
and define \(fX(u)=u\) and \(fZ(v)=v\). Degeneracy at \(p\in\{0,1\}\) or \(r\in\{0,1\}\) is allowed; thus no support condition is being added. For \((x,z,u,v)\in D^4\), define the required response probability
\[
h(x,z,u,v):=
\begin{cases}
t_{uv},&(x,z)=(0,0),\\
\gamma_A,&(x,z)=(1,0),\\
\gamma_B,&(x,z)=(0,1),\\
1/2,&(x,z)=(1,1).
\end{cases}
\]
Let
\[
\mathcal H:=\{t_{00},t_{01},t_{10},t_{11},
\gamma_A,\gamma_B,1/2\}.
\]
List the distinct elements of \(\mathcal H\cup\{0,1\}\) in increasing order as
\[
0=\lambda_0<\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_m=1.
\]
There are at most nine listed values, and hence \(m\le8\). Let \(W0\), independent of \((U0,V0)\), take values in \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with
\[
\mathbb P(W0=k)=\lambda_k-\lambda_{k-1},
\qquad 1\le k\le m.
\]
These probabilities are positive and telescope to one. If \(h=\lambda_j\) for \(0\le j\le m\), then
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{m}
\mathbf 1\{\lambda_k\le h\}
(\lambda_k-\lambda_{k-1})
=\sum_{k=1}^{j}(\lambda_k-\lambda_{k-1})
=\lambda_j=h.
\]
Thus the single deterministic structural function
\[
fY(x,z,u,v,k):=
\mathbf 1\{\lambda_k\le h(x,z,u,v)\}
\]
satisfies
\[
\mathbb P\{fY(x,z,u,v,W0)=1\}=h(x,z,u,v)
\]
for every \((x,z,u,v)\in D^4\). The construction uses one common \(fY\) in every intervention, and the product law makes \(U0,V0,W0\) mutually independent.

We now verify all eight supplied cells. Under \(\operatorname{do}(Z=0)\), independence and \(w_{ij}t_{ij}=n_{ij}\) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_M(X=0,Y=1\mid\operatorname{do}(Z=0))
&=w00t_{00}+w01t_{01}\\
&=n_{00}+n_{01}=c+(a-c)=a=A(0,1),
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_M(X=1,Y=1\mid\operatorname{do}(Z=0))
&=(1-p)\gamma_A=A(1,1).
\end{aligned}
\]
The induced row probabilities of \(X\) are \(p\) and \(1-p\). Normalization of \(A\) and the definition of \(p\) therefore give
\[
P_M(X=0,Y=0\mid\operatorname{do}(Z=0))
=p-a=A(0,0)
\]
and
\[
P_M(X=1,Y=0\mid\operatorname{do}(Z=0))
=1-p-A(1,1)=A(1,0).
\]
These identities remain valid when either row has probability zero.

Similarly, under \(\operatorname{do}(X=0)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_M(Z=0,Y=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X=0))
&=w00t_{00}+w10t_{10}\\
&=n_{00}+n_{10}=c+(b-c)=b=B(0,1),
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
P_M(Z=1,Y=1\mid\operatorname{do}(X=0))
=(1-r)\gamma_B=B(1,1).
\]
Since the induced row probabilities of \(Z\) are \(r\) and \(1-r\), normalization of \(B\) gives
\[
P_M(Z=0,Y=0\mid\operatorname{do}(X=0))
=r-b=B(0,0)
\]
and
\[
P_M(Z=1,Y=0\mid\operatorname{do}(X=0))
=1-r-B(1,1)=B(1,0).
\]
Thus the constructed model belongs to \(MC(A,B)\), including on all support faces.

Finally, under \(\operatorname{do}(X=0,Z=0)\), independence of the roots and the threshold identity give
\[
\begin{aligned}
q
&=\sum_{i,j\in D}\mathbb P(U0=i,V0=j)t_{ij}\\
&=\sum_{i,j\in D}w_{ij}t_{ij}\\
&=n_{00}+n_{01}+n_{10}+n_{11}\\
&=c+(a-c)+(b-c)+d=a+b-c+d.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the source-preserving lift directly, without a limiting argument and without any strict-positivity premise.

For each \((i,j)\in D^2\), set \(t_{ij}=n_{ij}/w_{ij}\) when \(w_{ij}>0\), and set \(t_{ij}=0\) when \(w_{ij}=0\). Set \(\gamma_A=A(1,1)/(1-p)\) when \(1-p>0\) and \(\gamma_A=0\) otherwise; set \(\gamma_B=B(1,1)/(1-r)\) when \(1-r>0\) and \(\gamma_B=0\) otherwise. Define \(h(x,z,u,v)\) to be \(t_{uv}\), \(\gamma_A\), \(\gamma_B\), or \(1/2\) according as \((x,z)\) equals \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\), or \((1,1)\). Order the distinct values of \(\{t_{00},t_{01},t_{10},t_{11},\gamma_A,\gamma_B,1/2,0,1\}\) as \(0=\lambda_0<\cdots<\lambda_m=1\); give the private root \(W0\) the law \(P(W0=k)=\lambda_k-\lambda_{k-1}\) on \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\); and define \(fY(x,z,u,v,k)=\mathbf 1\{\lambda_k\le h(x,z,u,v)\}\). Take independent \(D\)-valued roots \(U0,V0\) with \(P(U0=0)=p\), \(P(V0=0)=r\), and set \(fX(u)=u\), \(fZ(v)=v\).
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The previous handle did not specify how to construct response probabilities on zero-mass natural-treatment strata or null experimental rows. The corrected construction uses explicit zero-denominator branches and therefore names a finite object on the entire closed simplex.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed: On input normalized \(2\times2\) probability tables \((A,B)\), compute \((p,r,a,b)\), return incompatible exactly when either \(a-b<-(1-p)r\) or \(a-b>p(1-r)\), and otherwise return \((qL,qU)\) from their three-branch formulas. If all input cells are rational and the pair is compatible, also use \((c,d)=(cU,0)\) and \((c,d)=(cL,w11)\). For each endpoint pair set \(n_{00}=c\), \(n_{01}=a-c\), \(n_{10}=b-c\), and \(n_{11}=d\); set \(t_{ij}=n_{ij}/w_{ij}\) when \(w_{ij}>0\) and \(t_{ij}=0\) when \(w_{ij}=0\). Set \(\gamma_A=A(1,1)/(1-p)\) when \(1-p>0\) and \(\gamma_A=0\) when \(1-p=0\); set \(\gamma_B=B(1,1)/(1-r)\) when \(1-r>0\) and \(\gamma_B=0\) when \(1-r=0\). Use response probabilities \(t_{uv}\) when \((x,z)=(0,0)\), \(\gamma_A\) when \((x,z)=(1,0)\), \(\gamma_B\) when \((x,z)=(0,1)\), and \(1/2\) when \((x,z)=(1,1)\). Sort the distinct response probabilities together with \(\{0,1\}\) as \(0=\lambda_0<\cdots<\lambda_m=1\), give \(W0=k\) mass \(\lambda_k-\lambda_{k-1}\), take independent \(D\)-valued \(U0,V0\) with zero-probabilities \(p,r\), set \(fX(u)=u\), \(fZ(v)=v\), and set \(fY(x,z,u,v,k)=\mathbf 1\{\lambda_k\le h(x,z,u,v)\}\) for the specified response probability \(h\). Emit the resulting two models \(M\in MC(A,B)\) as lower- and upper-endpoint certificates.
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The certificate procedure previously divided by stratum and row probabilities without guarding the support faces. The corrected branches set the immaterial conditional response to zero whenever its denominator is zero, preserving rationality and the fixed support bound.

The strict-positivity version is subsumed by the proved closed-simplex lift. Replacing the node is necessary because the formal claim-change channel permits narrowing only, while this directive requires a genuine scope enlargement; inbound dependencies should migrate to the stronger theorem.

proposed.comparator_claim: When the generic finite discrete-SCM polynomial program is instantiated with the present product-disturbance graph, two experimental inputs, and target, its minimization and maximization give sharp lower and upper bounds.
Counterfactual consistency of overlapping categorical marginal SCMs restricts the admissible marginal and joint SCMs.
Every categorical SCM has a finite canonical SCM with the same graph and all the same counterfactual distributions.
EMCC returns fully specified compatible SCMs whose counterfactual range approximates the actual bounds from inside.
The global extrema of a response-function linear program occur at vertices of its feasible polytope.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The closed-simplex result is now a faithful same-input analytic specialization of the generic sharp discrete-SCM optimization theorem of Duarte et al.; the latter does not supply the present compatibility inequality, formulas, or small witnesses.

prose_updates.tldr: Two complete experiments on overlapping margins of a binary collider need not arise from one SCM. For arbitrary normalized binary tables, including structural-zero faces, the note proves an iff compatibility inequality and a closed-form sharp interval for the all-zero joint-intervention risk. A single finite ordered-threshold construction preserves the two independent source roots, uses one deterministic outcome law in every regime, and attains every feasible value with at most eight private-noise atoms. The result yields constant-time endpoints, exact rational endpoint certificates, and an optional conservative sampling interval for this fixed graph.

project_justification.fill: The project derives the two-mass fiber on the closed probability simplex, proves a source-preserving finite extension with explicit zero-denominator branches, and packages the resulting iff test and max--min interval as an exact analytic certificate for the same fixed input that Autobounds handles through generic polynomial optimization.

prose_updates.related_work: Gresele et al. formulate the structural causal marginal problem and show how one shared response-function law constrains overlapping causal models; their main analytic Boolean construction is causally sufficient, while their confounded extension retains a high-dimensional partially factorized law. Duarte et al. prove that sharp discrete causal bounds under observational and experimental evidence reduce to polynomial programs and implement the generic method in Autobounds. The present closed-simplex model, intervention menu, and target form a binary product-disturbance specialization within that scope, so the generic sharpness theorem applies to the corresponding optimization problem; it does not provide the graph-specific compatibility inequality, closed-form endpoints, or at-most-eight-atom common-SCM certificates derived here. Zhang, Tian, and Bareinboim prove finite canonical SCM sufficiency for arbitrary categorical counterfactual distributions; the present threshold lift is a smaller menu-specific certificate, not a generic canonicalization theorem. Sachs, Jonzon, Sjoelander, and Gabriel derive tight symbolic bounds for response-function models with linear constraints; their elimination logic is adjacent, while the independent latent-source structure here is preserved explicitly. Zaffalon et al. fuse heterogeneous observational and randomized studies through causal EM and report approximate inner ranges, making their work adjacent multi-source bounding rather than the exact analytic result proved here. Shridharan and Iyengar reduce the degree of multilinear causal-bound programs in quasi-Markovian graphs, while Finkelstein and Shpitser and Balke and Pearl supply related inequality and response-type templates; none of these checked results states the present closed-simplex formulas.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The source-preserving extension is proved on the entire closed simplex by explicit zero-mass branches; it does not rely on continuity from positive tables. Independence of the two source roots remains load-bearing: allowing them to be correlated can move the target outside the independent-source interval. The at-most-eight-atom construction is an upper certificate, not an optimal-support theorem, and the optional sampling interval is conservative rather than tie-optimal.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The result covers arbitrary normalized binary tables, including structural zeros, for exactly the collider graph, the two stated experimental regimes, mutually independent shared roots, private outcome noise, and the all-zero joint-intervention risk. Correlated or dependence-budget source roots, different study populations, a simultaneous region for all four joint-intervention risks, three or more parents, minimal support, nominal tie-robust inference, general thicket compilation, and any field-tier claim remain excluded. Any assertion of a strictly positive identified-set width is explicitly confined to the interior regime \(0<p,r<1\); no positive-width assertion is made on support faces. If regime \(B\) is omitted, the mass accounting gives \(q\in[a,a+1-p]\); symmetrically, omitting regime \(A\) gives \(q\in[b,b+1-r]\).

statement_notes.justification: The common threshold construction proves that every feasible mass pair lifts on every support face without coupling the two source roots.
statement_notes.gap: The lift is derived directly because generic finite canonicalization and generic polynomial-program sharpness do not themselves provide this explicit at-most-eight-point source-preserving certificate.
statement_notes.consumer: The theorem supplies the common-SCM attainment step for closed-simplex compatibility, sharpness, exact endpoint certificates, and an Autobounds specialization oracle.
